entities.summary:
The Zanzibar Revolution, also known as the Uprising of January 12, 1964, was a pivotal event in modern African history that marked the end of colonial rule in Zanzibar. This British protectorate had been a strategic trading hub and a thorn in the side of the newly independent Tanganyika. On January 12, 1964, a coalition of Chagga and Shirazi rebels, along with the Afro-Shirazi Party, overthrew the Sultan's government, citing corruption, poverty, and lack of democracy. The revolution was sparked by the rejection of the proposed merger with Tanganyika, which would have abolished Zanzibar's autonomy.

The revolutionaries quickly established a new government, led by Abeid Karume, who became the first President of Zanzibar. The new government nationalized key sectors of the economy, including banking and commerce, and implemented land reforms to redistribute property to the poor. The revolution also led to a significant increase in education and healthcare services, making Zanzibar one of the most socially progressive countries in Africa at the time.

The Zanzibar Revolution had a lasting impact on the region, inspiring similar movements across East Africa. It also paved the way for the eventual merger of Zanzibar and Tanganyika in 1964, which became the modern-day United Republic of Tanzania. The revolution's legacy can be seen in the country's commitment to social justice, education, and healthcare, which continues to shape the nation's development to this day.

As Abeid Karume famously said, 'We have thrown out the colonial masters, and now we are going to build a new society, a society of equality, of justice, of freedom.'
